sets.label: basic / backyard host for a crowd / buffet heat

metadata.description: Does the host shorten the time limit in hot weather and avoid mixing batches?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Time limits get shorter in the heat, because bacteria multiply faster in warm air. Small pans that are replaced often keep food hot and fresh, and the rest stays hot until it is needed.
Two hours is the usual limit, but it drops to about an hour when it is hot out. Food left in the heat can pass its safe time before the two hours are up.
Mixing fresh meat into an old pan puts the fresh food on the clock of the old. Replace the pan with a fresh one instead of topping it up.
Reheating does not undo every kind of risk, since some bacteria leave toxins that heat does not remove. Keep to the time limits instead of relying on reheating.

metadata.description: Does the learner store raw meat so it cannot contaminate other food?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Raw juices can carry bacteria. A sealed container on the bottom shelf keeps them from dripping onto food that will be eaten without more cooking.
Anything that drips from a top-shelf package lands on the food below. Raw meat belongs on the bottom shelf, in a container.
Open raw meat next to cooked food invites cross-contamination. Keep raw meat sealed and below ready-to-eat food.
Rinsing raw meat splashes bacteria around the sink and counter, and does not make the meat safer. Leave it unrinsed and wrapped.

metadata.description: Does the learner know why ground meat needs a higher minimum?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Grinding spreads whatever is on the surface through the whole patty, so the center needs to be thoroughly cooked. 160°F is the safe minimum for ground beef, checked in the center.
145°F applies to whole cuts of beef, where bacteria sit on the surface. In ground meat they are mixed through, so the minimum is higher, 160°F.
Smoking at home does not preserve meat or make it safe at lower temperatures. Cook ground beef to 160°F in the center.
Color does not reliably show doneness in ground meat. A patty can brown before it is safe. Use a thermometer.

metadata.description: Does the learner prepare the surface and avoid rinsing raw meat?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A damp surface steams instead of building a crust, and rub slides off. Patting it dry helps the seasoning cling and the bark develop. Do it with paper towels, then wash your hands.
Rinsing raw meat does not make it safer and splashes bacteria around the sink and counter. Cooking to the right temperature takes care of bacteria.
Soaking adds surface water and washes away flavor. Moisture inside comes from the cook and the cut, not from a bath.
Seasoning only on the outside after cooking misses the chance to build a bark. Seasoning before the cook lets the rub set in and form the crust.

metadata.description: Does the learner keep brining meat cold?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Brining takes hours, and that is long enough for bacteria to grow if the meat is warm. The refrigerator keeps it cold throughout. A lidded container keeps the raw juices from spreading.
Salt slows some bacteria but does not make a counter safe for hours of soaking. Brine in the refrigerator.
Outdoor and garage temperatures swing and are hard to trust. The refrigerator holds a known safe temperature.
Warm water puts the meat straight into the danger zone for hours. Dissolve the salt, cool the brine and keep everything cold.

metadata.description: Does the learner know how to test a thermometer?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A slushy bath of ice and water sits at the freezing point whatever the weather or altitude, so it is a dependable test. If the reading is off, adjust it if the thermometer allows, or replace it.
Boiling water also works. The catch is that the boiling point drops as altitude rises, so you have to know your local value. The ice bath avoids that problem.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: a valid test with a known caveat, so a good answer but not the simplest.

connections.feedback: Room air is not a controlled reference, and it changes through the day. Use ice water, which stays at a known temperature.
Thermometers can be off from new, can drift, and can be knocked out of true by a drop. A quick ice-water check before important cooks takes seconds.

metadata.description: Does the learner know that more smoke is not better?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Meat takes up the most smoke early, and too much wood makes heavy, bitter smoke. A few small pieces on a clean fire give plenty of flavor. Adjust to taste next time.
Meat does not need to sit in thick smoke. Heavy smoke tends to taste harsh. Thin, clean smoke is the goal.
Green wood holds a lot of water and smolders and steams, which makes sour, heavy smoke. Use seasoned, dry wood.
Smoke is mostly absorbed early in the cook, so a steady stream of wood through the whole cook adds little and risks bitter smoke. Add wood early and let the cook run.

metadata.description: Does the learner see that wood schedules are a matter of school?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Meat takes up the most smoke early, and too much wood makes heavy, bitter smoke. A few small pieces on a clean fire give plenty of flavor, and you can tune the amount to taste.

Some cooks keep a trickle of wood going through the cook, especially in a leaky cooker where smoke disperses. It can work if the smoke stays thin and clean. Many find that most of the benefit comes early.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: wood schedules are a matter of school and equipment, and the chief test is whether the smoke stays thin and clean.

connections.feedback: Heavy smoke is not a sign of more flavor and tends to leave a harsh coating. Keep it thin and pale.
Fresh-cut wood is full of moisture and smolders and steams instead of burning cleanly. Use seasoned, dry wood.

metadata.description: Does the learner pull while warm?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Warm meat shreds easily as the fat and connective tissue are still soft, and a short rest makes it comfortable to handle. Use clean gloves, and discard any hard bits of fat or gristle.
Chilling and reheating works if you chill it quickly and heat it thoroughly. It makes shredding harder and can dry the meat, so it suits a make-ahead plan rather than a first choice.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: a legitimate make-ahead method with a texture cost.

connections.feedback: Piping hot meat is too hot to handle, and the steam and juices burn hands. Give it a short rest first.
Cooled meat firms up and is much harder to shred, and the surface dries. Pull while it is still warm.

metadata.description: Does the learner starve a flare-up of air?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Flames need air, so closing the lid and vents starves them. Keep your face and arms clear of the opening, and use long tongs and heat-proof gloves when you have to touch anything. If fire spreads beyond the cooker, step back and call for help.
Water on burning grease can spit and spread it, and cause steam burns. Cut off the air.
A wide open lid feeds the flames more oxygen and can make them leap higher and closer to you. Close the lid instead.
A towel can catch fire and put your hand at risk next to the flames. Cut off the air with the lid and vents.

metadata.description: Does the learner connect dryness to overcooking lean meat?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Lean breast meat has little fat, and the further past the safe minimum it goes, the more moisture it loses. Pull it as soon as the thickest part gets there, and rest it briefly.
Smoke adds flavor and does not change how juicy the meat is. Dryness comes from how far the meat cooked.
Undercooked chicken is pale and wet, not dry and stringy. At 185°F the meat is far past the safe minimum.
A brine does help lean meat hold more moisture, and it is a good habit. It narrows the margin for overcooking and does not remove it, so pulling at the right temperature still matters.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: brining helps and many cooks swear by it, but it is not the main explanation for a result at 185°F.

sets.label: basic / backyard host for a crowd / kids zone

metadata.description: Does the host keep children and pets away from the fire?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Cookers, flames, hot surfaces and ash are burn hazards, and children move quickly. A marked-off zone on stable ground keeps them away and keeps the cooker from being bumped.
Tending a fire is for adults. Placing the cooker beside the play area invites a burn or a tip-over.
A blanket can catch fire or trap heat, and a cooker left uncovered by a distracted adult is still a hazard. Mark off an area and keep children out of it.
A garage doorway collects fumes and is a fire risk. Keep the cooker outdoors in the open, in a marked-off space.

metadata.description: Does the learner understand a slow-spreading fire?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: The lit coals ignite the unlit ones a few at a time, so the temperature stays steady for hours with no restart. It is a common setup for low-and-slow cooking on a kettle.
Lighting only a few coals means the cooker takes longer to reach temperature. The benefit is in how long the fire lasts.
Smoldering coals are a sign of poor airflow and bitter smoke. This setup is about a long steady burn, not heavy smoke.
This setup is for holding a low steady heat for hours. A hot searing fire needs a lot of coals lit at once.

metadata.description: Does the learner know the behaviors of the two charcoal types?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Briquettes are pressed to a uniform size, so they burn evenly and predictably, which is handy for long, steady cooks. Lump is charred wood in irregular pieces that lights quickly and burns hotter and faster.
That has it backward. Briquettes are the pressed ones, made of crushed charcoal and binder, and lump is charred wood in irregular pieces.
How clean the burn is depends on what is in the fuel and how it is lit, not on the type alone. Lighting with a chimney starter and waiting for ash matters more.
They burn differently. Briquettes are steadier and more even, and lump is hotter and quicker. Each cooks differently, so adjust the airflow and the amount.
